name: Network pivoting & tunnelling (§3)
description: Turn a proven foothold into reach onto an internal segment: a chisel or ligolo-ng SOCKS/TUN tunnel, sshuttle, an SSH dynamic forward, then enumerate the far side through the proxy. Every tunnel puts traffic on the wire, so each pauses for approval; a confirmed pivot widens scope to the subnet it exposes, scope grows, it is never skipped.

actions.title: Chisel Reverse SOCKS Tunnel
actions.hypothesis: When the foothold can see an internal subnet, a reverse SOCKS proxy served by chisel routes your attacker-box tooling through the compromised host and onto that segment.
actions.proves: a working SOCKS tunnel into the network the foothold sits on
actions.does_not_prove: that any particular internal host is reachable, only a scan through the tunnel shows that

actions.title: Ligolo-ng Tunnel + Route
actions.hypothesis: ligolo-ng builds a TUN-interface pivot: once the agent connects back you add a route for the discovered subnet and internal hosts answer as if directly attached.
actions.proves: a routed pivot onto the foothold's network
actions.does_not_prove: that any specific internal host is reachable until a scan confirms it

actions.title: sshuttle Transparent Pivot
actions.hypothesis: Given working SSH credentials on the foothold, sshuttle carries a whole subnet over that SSH session transparently, with no proxychains or client-side proxy setup.
actions.proves: a transparent route onto the foothold's subnet carried over SSH
actions.does_not_prove: that any given host is reachable until a scan confirms it

actions.title: SSH Dynamic Port-Forward (SOCKS)
actions.hypothesis: `ssh -D` on its own stands up a SOCKS proxy through the foothold, the no-extra-tooling pivot whenever SSH credentials are already in hand.
actions.proves: a SOCKS proxy onto the foothold's network
actions.does_not_prove: that any specific host is reachable until a scan confirms it

actions.title: Scan an Internal Host Through the Pivot
actions.hypothesis: Once a tunnel is up, enumerate the far side exactly as you did the first host. Through a SOCKS tunnel (chisel, ssh -D) wrap a TCP-connect nmap in proxychains; through a routed tunnel (ligolo, sshuttle) the subnet is a normal route, so nmap runs unmodified. Either way, this turns 'the tunnel is up' into real attack surface on an internal host.
actions.proves: open ports on an internal host reached across the pivot
actions.does_not_prove: a vulnerability, this maps attack surface and nothing more

commands.note: SOCKS tunnel (chisel / ssh -D): a SOCKS proxy cannot carry nmap's raw SYN scan, so use -sT (TCP connect). UDP and ICMP will not traverse it.
Routed tunnel (ligolo / sshuttle): the subnet is a real route, so nmap runs unmodified — no proxychains, and a normal -sV service scan works.

actions.title: DNS Tunnel for Egress-Restricted Hosts
actions.hypothesis: When a foothold can resolve DNS but every other outbound port is filtered, DNS itself becomes your transport. A DNS tunnel encodes data in queries to a domain whose authoritative server you control, giving a slow interactive channel or a tunnel for other tools when nothing else gets out. dnscat2 or iodine run a server on your box and a client on the target. Reach for it only when the faster transports (a reverse shell, an SSH tunnel) are blocked.
actions.proves: a working data channel over DNS from an otherwise egress-filtered host
actions.does_not_prove: a channel where the host cannot resolve arbitrary external names

report.finding: DNS tunnel established from egress-restricted host

commands.note: Test the fast transports first; a DNS tunnel is slow, so use it only when a reverse shell and an SSH tunnel are both blocked.
The server listens on your attacker box as the handler for a domain delegated to you.
The client on the target encodes its traffic into queries for your domain, which the server decodes into a session.
Use the session as a shell or forward a port through it; the normal pivoting workflow applies, over DNS.

actions.title: SSH Local / Remote Port Forward (-L / -R)
actions.hypothesis: When you only need one internal service rather than a whole subnet, a single SSH port forward is simpler and quieter than a SOCKS proxy. `ssh -L` binds a port on your box to an internal host:port reached from the foothold, so your tools connect to localhost. `ssh -R` does the reverse, exposing a port of your attacker box to the internal network, which lands a callback when the foothold cannot reach you directly. Both ride an existing SSH session, so no extra tooling touches the target.
actions.proves: a direct route to one internal service, forwarded over the SSH session
actions.does_not_prove: reach to the rest of the subnet, each forward exposes exactly the one port you name

commands.note: Local forward: your localhost:8080 now reaches the internal web service through the foothold.
Remote forward: exposes your attacker-box listener on the foothold, for a callback when it cannot reach you directly.

actions.title: Sweep the Adjacent Hosts
actions.hypothesis: The foothold's ARP/neighbour cache already named the live hosts on its segments - you do not have to guess the subnet. Scan exactly those IPs: lead with an nxc protocol sweep to spot SMB/WinRM and where your credential already works, then a full nmap for the rest of the surface. Run it straight from the foothold if they share a segment, or through your tunnel from Kali if they do not.
actions.proves: the live attack surface of the adjacent hosts the neighbour cache named
actions.does_not_prove: a vulnerability or any access on them, only which ports and services are exposed

commands.note: PREFERRED: sweep the neighbour IPs over SMB in one shot — it fingerprints OS/domain/signing and, once you add -u/-p, marks every host the credential opens. Pass a space-separated list or a targets file.

Full service scan of the same hosts. If they are only reachable through the pivot, prefix with proxychains (SOCKS tunnel) or run it after a routed tunnel is up — build one from the connectivity panel's tunnel wizard first.
The through-a-SOCKS-tunnel form when the neighbours sit on a subnet you can only reach via the foothold.

actions.title: Reach an Internal-Only Service
actions.hypothesis: A service bound to 127.0.0.1 or an internal NIC is invisible from your box but wide open from the foothold - databases, admin panels and message queues hide here constantly. The listener list told you the exact port; forward it out (ssh -L, or a chisel/ligolo forward) and your tools hit it on localhost as if it were local. This is how a localhost-only MySQL or an internal web admin becomes reachable.
actions.proves: a reachable path from your box to an internal-only service the foothold was listening on
actions.does_not_prove: a vulnerability in that service, only that you can now talk to it

commands.note: The quickest forward when you hold SSH on the foothold: localhost:{{local_port}} on Kali now reaches the internal service. No extra tooling touches the target. For a non-SSH foothold, build a chisel/ligolo forward from the connectivity panel's tunnel wizard instead.
Confirm the forwarded service answers, then point the matching tool (mysql, a browser, impacket) at localhost:{{local_port}} and enumerate it like any other host.

actions.title: Interrogate the Internal Resolver
actions.hypothesis: The foothold's own resolver is almost always a domain controller, and it will name the rest of the estate for you. Ask it for the DC locator SRV records and try a zone transfer: in an AD environment this single step hands you the domain name and every DC - unlocking the whole AD attack lane - often before you hold a single credential. The resolver's address came straight from the foothold's DNS config.
actions.proves: the AD domain and its domain controllers, read from the internal resolver
actions.does_not_prove: a credential or any access, this is name resolution — the DCs it names still have to be attacked

commands.note: The DC locator: every domain controller registers this SRV record, so the answer section lists them by name. _kerberos._tcp.{{domain}} and _gc._tcp.{{domain}} (global catalog) work the same way.
A full zone transfer. Most resolvers refuse it, but a misconfigured one dumps every A record in the domain — an instant host inventory. If AXFR is refused you still have the SRV answers above.
The Windows-friendly form of the same DC-locator query, for when dig is not to hand.
